::::::: {.tldr}
[TL;DR]{.tldr-label}

:::::: {.tldr-cards}
::: {.tldr-card .part-1}
[Part I · Self-reference](#part-1){.tldr-link}

A model evaluated against the annotator who labeled its training data looks better than it would against an independent annotator. We show that this holds on average over annotators in theory, and our tests detect it in real chest X-ray annotations from VinDr-CXR.
:::

::: {.tldr-card .part-2}
[Part II · Continuous](#part-2){.tldr-link}

A panel of reference annotators is reliable for a model–human comparison if it reaches the same conclusion as the latent target. We develop a test that identifies reliable panels without observing the latent target and controls the probability of a false certification, and we apply it to real chest X-ray annotations from VinDr-CXR.
:::

::: {.tldr-card .part-3}
[Part III · Bernoulli](#part-3){.tldr-link}

For binary labels, annotator bias is modeled on the logit scale, so the test of [Part II](#part-2) requires a new, more conservative bound on $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}.$ Since our real-data setting (R11–R16) offers at most four reference annotators, we evaluate the test on synthetic labels generated for a larger pool of annotators on VinDr-CXR images. On these semi-synthetic data, the certification rate of the modified test increases with the number of reference annotators.
:::
::::::
:::::::

## Introduction {#introduction}

Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly being used to assist with or automate tasks that have traditionally relied on human annotation and expert judgment. Examples include interpreting medical images [@aggarwal2021diagnostic], identifying harmful or toxic online content [@gorwa2020algorithmic], and evaluating or ranking generated responses [@ouyang2022training]. For these tasks, human annotations often provide the supervision used to train the models [@prabhakaran2024grasp; @uma2021learning].

However, these tasks are usually subjective, so the labels used to train a model depend on the judgments of the human annotators. For example, annotators may disagree about whether a text contains hate speech or which emotion it expresses [@rottger2022two; @davani2022dealing]. Human preferences also enter language-model training through demonstrations and comparisons between responses, as in InstructGPT [@ouyang2022training]. A related issue arises in medical imaging: radiologists may disagree about findings in the same chest X-ray, so the reference label can depend on which radiologists assess it [@abdalla2023hurdles]. 
When annotators' judgments leave consistent patterns in the labels they provide, this is commonly referred to as *annotation bias* [@geva2019we; @wich-etal-2020-investigating].

Such systematic bias in annotation can affect the performance comparisons between trained models and human annotators (hereafter *model–human comparisons*). These comparisons have attracted considerable attention in medical imaging [@liu2019comparison; @nagendran2020artificial; @ahmad2023machine]. For example, in chest X-ray interpretation, @irvin2019chexpert reports that its model outperformed individual radiologists on several findings, while @wu2020comparison reports higher specificity and precision for an AI model than for radiology residents. Both studies used reference labels established by panels of specialists through majority voting or consensus. However, the former study did not report whether the training annotators overlapped with the reference experts, while in the latter, one of the reference experts was also involved in training. Now we use a simple model to explain how annotation bias can affect model–human comparisons under this overlap.

::: {#intro-bias .ab-result .intro-bias}
::: {.ab-widget data-widget="intro-bias"}
This interactive figure requires JavaScript.
:::

[Errors of the model and of annotator B on a single image $x,$ with latent truth $Y^*(x)=0$ and no annotation noise. Annotator A labels the image $Y_A(x)=Y^*(x)+b_A(x);$ the model trained on A predicts $\widehat Y_A(x)=Y_A(x)+\widehat e_A(x)$ with learning error $\widehat e_A(x)=0.1;$ annotator B labels it $Y_B(x)=Y^*(x)+b_B(x)$ with $b_B(x)=0.3.$ Each error is the distance to the reference: annotator A on the left, as in @eq-intro-self-ref, and the latent truth on the right, as in @eq-intro-latent-ref. Drag the slider to change A's bias $b_A(x).$]{.ab-caption}
:::

Denoting the label given by an annotator $i$ on object $x$ as $Y_i(x)$ and the corresponding latent truth as $Y^*(x),$ we write
$$Y_i(x) = Y^*(x) + b_i(x) + \epsilon_{i,x},$$
where $b_i(x)$ is the systematic bias of annotator $i$ and $\epsilon_{i,x}$ is the noise. Suppose a model $\widehat Y_A$ is trained on annotator A and compared with annotator B. Assume the reference is again the annotator A and the comparison is on dataset $\mathcal{D}.$ Then the model–human comparison is between 
$\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat Y_A (x) - Y_A (x) ||$ and $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || Y_B (x) - Y_A (x) ||,$
which can also be written as @eq-intro-self-ref on the left below. Similarly, when the latent truth is chosen as the reference, we can rewrite the actual model–human comparison, between $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||\widehat Y_A (x) - Y^*(x)||$ and $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||Y_B (x) - Y^*(x)||$ as @eq-intro-latent-ref on the right.

:::: {.eq-pair}
::: {.eq-col}
[Annotator A as reference]{.eq-col-title}

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat e_A (x) \mathbin{\textcolor{#A3A9AF}{+}} \textcolor{#A3A9AF}{\cancel{b_A(x)}} \mathbin{\textcolor{#A3A9AF}{-}} \textcolor{#A3A9AF}{\cancel{b_A(x)}} - \epsilon_{A,x} || \\
\mathrm{versus} \\
\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||\big(b_B(x) - \textcolor{#B5482E}{b_A(x)}\big) + \epsilon_{B,x} - \epsilon_{A,x}||
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-intro-self-ref}
:::

::: {.eq-col}
[Latent truth as reference]{.eq-col-title}

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat e_A (x) + \textcolor{#B5482E}{b_A(x)} || \\
\mathrm{versus} \\
\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||b_B(x) + \epsilon_{B,x} ||
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-intro-latent-ref}
:::
::::

Here $\widehat e_A (x)$ captures the approximation error and training error arising from finite samples and incomplete optimization, and the rewrite holds under mild conditions^[Sufficient conditions are that $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{A,x}\mid x]=0$ and that MSE is used as the training loss.]. The comparison in @eq-intro-self-ref may favor the model's performance relative to that in @eq-intro-latent-ref: the bias term $b_A$ cancels from the error of the model $\widehat Y_A$ and instead enters the error of the human annotator $Y_B.$

Aside from the analysis above, previous work has also shown that models can learn systematic tendencies in how individual annotators label data [@binns2017like; @geva2019we; @nichyporuk2022rethinking]. A reported model advantage may therefore reflect, in part, agreement with the reference's annotation patterns. However, several questions remain open, particularly in real-world medical applications:

::::: {.question-cards}
::: {.question-card}
**To what extent does annotation bias affect model–human comparisons?**

[Part I →](#part-1){.question-link}
:::

::: {.question-card}
**Could accounting for this bias reverse the conclusion?**

[Part II →](#part-2){.question-link}
:::

::: {.question-card}
**How can we identify an annotator whose labels can serve as a reliable reference for such comparisons?**

[Part II →](#part-2){.question-link} [Part III →](#part-3){.question-link}
:::
:::::

To address these questions, we focus on predicting thoracic abnormalities from chest X-rays using the VinDr-CXR dataset [@PhysioNet-vindr-cxr-1.0.0; @nguyen2022vindr], accessed through PhysioNet [@pollard_physionet_2026], which provides independent annotations from multiple radiologists for the same images. We train models on individual radiologists' labels and compare their performance with that of other radiologists under different evaluation references. This setting allows us to examine how the choice of training annotator and evaluation reference affects the conclusions of model–human comparisons.

## Conclusion {#conclusion}

This article examines how the choice of evaluation reference affects model–human comparisons when the reference labels come from annotators with systematic biases. [Part I](#part-1) studies the self-reference effect, where a model is evaluated against the annotator whose labels it is trained on. Since the model has learned the reference annotator's own bias, only the human is penalized for it, which tilts the comparison toward the model. 
Theoretically, this effect is expected to be nonnegative on average over randomly drawn annotators. Our tests further detect it for specific radiologists in VinDr-CXR, both for the aggregate score and for individual findings.

Since evaluating against independent reference annotators may bring in their own biases, for the aggregate score, [Part II](#part-2) develops a test that assesses whether an evaluation reference is reliable for a given model–human comparison. The reference is certified as reliable when it identifies the same better performer as the latent target. Two features make the test practical. First, it does not require the latent target: it bounds how much the evaluation reference can distort the comparison from how the reference annotators differ from one another. Second, it does not require the reference annotators to have labeled every evaluation image, since the evaluation reference is built from surrogate predictors trained on each annotator's available labels. Applied to six radiologists in VinDr-CXR, the test certifies more configurations as the number of reference annotators grows: at a total error budget of $0.20$, the certification rate rises from $10\%$ with two reference annotators to $23.3\%$ with three and $46.7\%$ with four.

For binary labels, where annotator bias acts on the logit scale, [Part III](#part-3) extends the test with a new, more conservative bound. On semi-synthetic labels generated for many annotators on VinDr-CXR images, the certification rate again increases with the number of reference annotators, but varies widely across findings: with $32$ reference annotators and a total error budget of $0.20$, it ranges from $0\%$ for Atelectasis to $95.8\%$ for Rib fracture. Certification is harder for findings on which the surrogate predictors differ more in their average logits.

What our framework can establish is limited by the available data. Testing the self-reference effect requires three annotators to label the same large set of items, a requirement that can be difficult to meet. It also requires a sufficient number of annotators, each with enough labeled data from the same distribution. Beyond these data requirements, the test has greater power for aggregate scores than for binary labels, for which the bound no longer relies on a Gaussian assumption on each reference annotator’s effect and is therefore conservative. A distributional assumption on this effect, as in the aggregate-score setting, would tighten this bound and improve power. Finally, data with verified ground truth would allow us to evaluate the test’s power and false certification rate on real tasks.
Beyond model–human comparisons, a natural next step is to extend the framework to model evaluation in general. Whenever human annotations serve as the reference for model evaluation, for example in measuring a single model's performance or ranking several models, annotation errors and disagreements can distort the conclusion [@gordon2021disagreement; @northcutt2021pervasive]. Analogous tests could determine whether an annotator-based reference reaches the same conclusion as the latent target.

```{=html}
<script>
// Local preview only: reload when the rendered page changes on disk.
// Quarto's own preview reload does not fire reliably here; this checks the
// served page once a second and reloads after it has settled on a new version.
(function () {
  var host = location.hostname;
  if (location.protocol !== "http:" || (host !== "localhost" && host !== "127.0.0.1")) return;
  var baseline = null;
  var candidate = null;
  var KEY = "ab-preview-state";

  // Remember the open Part and the scroll position across a preview reload.
  function activeTab() {
    var panes = document.querySelectorAll("#research-parts > .tab-content > .tab-pane");
    for (var i = 0; i < panes.length; i++) if (panes[i].classList.contains("active")) return i;
    return 0;
  }
  function saveAndReload() {
    try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify({ tab: activeTab(), y: window.pageYOffset })); } catch (e) {}
    location.reload();
  }
  var saved = null;
  try { saved = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) || "null"); sessionStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
  if (saved) {
    if ("scrollRestoration" in history) history.scrollRestoration = "manual";
    window.addEventListener("load", function () {
      var btn = document.querySelectorAll('#research-parts > ul.nav-tabs [data-bs-toggle="tab"]')[saved.tab];
      if (btn && window.bootstrap && window.bootstrap.Tab) window.bootstrap.Tab.getOrCreateInstance(btn).show();
      function restore() { window.scrollTo(0, saved.y); }
      restore();
      [100, 500, 1200].forEach(function (t) { setTimeout(restore, t); });
    });
  }

  function digest(text) {
    var h = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < text.length; i++) h = (h * 31 + text.charCodeAt(i)) | 0;
    return text.length + ":" + h;
  }
  function check() {
    fetch(location.pathname, { cache: "no-store" })
      .then(function (r) { return r.ok ? r.text() : null; })
      .then(function (text) {
        if (text === null) return;
        var d = digest(text);
        if (baseline === null || d === baseline) { baseline = baseline || d; candidate = null; return; }
        if (d === candidate) { saveAndReload(); } else { candidate = d; }
      })
      .catch(function () {})
      .then(function () { setTimeout(check, 1000); });
  }
  setTimeout(check, 1000);
})();
</script>
```
